analytic.title: Mapping and Priority Assignment for Real-Time Network-on-chip with Static and Dynamic Applications

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Networks-On-Chip (NoC) has emerged as a solution for addressing the limitation of bus-based communication in multi-processor system designs. Some of these systems are designed for executing real-time services which are associated with deadlines, failing to meet these deadlines may lead to failure of the system. The problem of Task Mapping and Priority assignment becomes more crucial when multiple applications are targeted on a platform in realtime scenario. Real-time schedulability analysis is performed assuming worst case scenario to get the lower bound of schedulability for tasks and flows. The term schedulability defines the number of tasks and flows meeting the deadlines. A broader range of Embedded System consists of both static and dynamic applications. The resources for static and dynamic applications are to be allocated separately. Considering mixed requirement of static and dynamic application and with major focus on dynamic scenario in real-time system, a novel approach for mapping and flow priority assignment has been reported in this paper. It extends the state of the art works in Deadline and Energy Aware Dynamic Mapping and Scheduling (DEAMS) algorithm with flow priority assignment approach obtained by modifying Graph based Exhaustive Search Algorithm (GESA). Current DEAMS algorithm does not consider the network congestion and flow priorities while mapping the tasks instances. In order to get better schedulability in dynamic scenarios, GESA has been modified to work in dynamic situations, which considers the flow dependencies as well. The graph based algorithm puts check for schedulability in a more deterministic way, making it more appropriate for real-time systems. The motivation behind the work presented in this paper lies in probable application of Cyber Physical Systems, having static and dynamic resource allocation for applications in real-time.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Network-on-chip (NoC) is a paradigm shift for communication of cores in Multi-Processor System [1]. In NoC based platform cores communicate through routing mechanism which provide scalability and reusability [2]. Task mapping on cores for maximization of core utilization while minimization of communication cost and energy consumption is important aspect for NoC driven multi-core design. Also, in real-time systems, additional measures like task response times and flow end-to-end latencies are to be considered. Embedded Systems are mostly real-time in nature that is designed to meet application specific requirements. Multi-processor systems are commonly used for Design of such Systems [3]. The situation becomes more crucial when multiple applications are targeted on a realtime platform. Examples for this are available in different Cyber Physical Systems such as Avionics Computer on which basic Navigation, Mission management, weapon aiming and ballistic computation are targeted. In this system, basic navigation is the permanent application while other applications come and depart as per the requirement of Mission Plan. The scenarios of dynamic applications are known a priori and required to be performed in exactly realtime bounds on arrival into system. Mapping process determines appropriate processing core for tasks execution of an application. Mapping of tasks depend on how task communicate and topology of connection of different processing element on the target system. Static mapping techniques are primarily based on evolutionary algorithms and meta-heuristics which are used mainly at time of design. These techniques provide good solutions but incur high run time. Because of higher cost of computation, these techniques are having question mark for use in dynamic applications [4]. Real-time System having dynamic requirement are required to take decision about task mapping and scheduling of dynamic tasks in addition to existing tasks [5]. Task Mapping is strongly related to scheduling in case of implementation of real-time NoC and governed by dependencies of tasks in task graph and connectivity of processing core in selected topology of NoC.

The referred DEAMS algorithms [6] deal with this type dynamic scenario. As per the requirements, the scheduling algorithm used is on-line and have low run-time cost with computationally simple heuristics. Focusing on dynamic scenario in real-time system, a novel approach for mapping and priority assignment has been explored in this paper. It extends the DEAMS algorithm discussed in [6] by adding graph based priority assignment approach GESA [7]. The graph based algorithm put check for schedulability in more deterministic way, making it more appropriate for real-time systems. For static part of application, task mapping is done by DEAMS and flow priority assignment is done using heuristics. Contribution of this paper as extension to DEAMS is as follows:

1. The paper addresses the problem domain having both static and dynamic applications. 2. It follows the task mapping criteria in DEAMS, so it is as energy efficient as DEAMS [6]. 3. For better schedulability in dynamic scenarios, GESA [7] has been modified to work in dynamic situations. 4. For better schedulability in static scenarios, heuristics has been used for flow priority assignment. 5. DEAMS is deadline aware, while this modified revision is deadline guaranteed. With respect to NoC topology and architectures, most widely used mesh topology for 2D NoCs has been considered in the paper. NoC with wormhole packet switching technique is extensively used because of its reduced buffer usage [8]. Virtual Channels (VCs) in routers allow multiple packets to access the same physical channel, and the router decides which packet to forward base on some arbitration policy. In RT-NoC, transmission of packet from source to destination over network is time bounded, means all the communication flows guarantee the packet delivery within required deadline for correct timely result. Employing such architectural considerations and combining response-time equations for tasks with latency equations for flows [9], analysis for guarantee of time bound behaviour in NoC based system can be performed [10]. Task mapping play a major role in deciding response time, latencies and ultimately application schedulability. Assigning optimal priorities to flows so that maximum numbers of flows are schedulable along with mapping is crucial in real-time NoC design. In Real-Time Network-on-chip, traffic-flows are marked schedulable, if all the packets of traffic-flows provide time bounded response irrespective of order of arrival of packets. Prediction of latencies is important to support the deadline bounds as latencies are partially non-deterministic due to network contention in real-time NoC. Latency can be because of multiple tasks getting assigned to same core or priorities of flows. Tasks are assigned to cores of platform and share information as per their execution and periodicity. During packet transfer the resources are shared and may result in contention when try to access same links or buffers. Network routers are designed with scheme of arbitration and serve only one packet at a time which cause suspension or delay for others.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section II describes the literature review and related work. Section III discusses mathematical foundation of schedulability analysis for real-time NoC. Section IV discusses about DEAMS Algorithm and its implementation. Section V discusses experimental work covering concept of GESA from task graphs to assignment of priorities along with mapping. Section VI contains a detailed comparison and results of experimental work. Conclusions and future work are presented in Section VII.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: This section presents a review of literature on task mapping and priority assignment in the domain of NoC based MPSoC. An application is specified by a task graph. When it is mapped over cores, selection of appropriate processing elements for the execution of tasks is decided by the mapping. Static mapping is determined at design time and cannot be changed during the run-time while dynamic mapping can be changed as and when tasks complete execution [4]. Static mapping techniques explored so far, have been done based on evolutionary techniques like GA, PSO, SA and supported by Heuristics. In [11], for mapping of task minimization of Manhattan distances has been considered to reduce cost of communication.

Dynamic mapping techniques use the run time heuristics to find the solution faster. Run-time heuristics are used for dynamic mapping for faster execution time. In [12], one of such technique is used to perform mapping. This technique assigns an available PE to a new task as soon as the new task arrive and available for execution. With the problem of static and dynamic mappings in case of NoC, various scheduling strategies have been adopted. In [13], scheduling has been considered along with minimization of energy and real time constraint. In [14], it has been presented that none of the earlier priority assignment policies work well for assigning priorities to communications in wormhole switched networks. A heuristic based branch and bound search algorithm (HSA) has been introduced to find the possible priority ordering for flows. In comparison to the traditional exhaustive algorithm which has exponential complexity, the HSA is much faster with the price of missing certain schedulable cases. In [16], priority assignment is performed using graph based algorithms GESA and GHSA. Undirected graph based techniques reduces the search space in comparison to HAS. It converts the task graph to flow graph and exploits the dependencies of flows and expected interference in network. The results in [16] presents that the GESA perform better than HAS in term of schedulability, but exhaustive search take longer time. GHSA perform same as HSA in term of schedulability, but improve timing performance significantly. Worst Case schedulability analysis, used widely for mapping and priority assignment, was first established in the base work of Shi and Burns [9].

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: This paper has considered NoC topology: 2D mesh (consisting of PEs, routers and links). A special purpose PE runs the Real Time Executive (RTE) and Task Manager, while general purpose PEs are for executing tasks. Mapping and scheduling for tasks of incoming application to appropriate resources are done by the manager core in runtime. The resource occupancy status of each PE is updated at run-time to provide the Manager Core with latest status about the resource availability. A PE can execute only one task at a time even though multiple tasks might be allocated to it. Deterministic XY routing has been assumed for implementation. Typical application model representation is done by task set and communication of messages between tasks which are characterized by computation and communication load imposed by an application. It is assumed that a message from task will be transmitted only after its execution is completed and overhead of the network interface is negligible. Before transmission, each message is packetized into one or several packets. A traffic flow represents a series of packets sent over the NoC from source task to destination task. Every task T is described as a T={c, t, p, d} tuple. Each task has a worst-case execution time (c), inter-arrival interval (t), priority (p) and deadline (d).

Similarly every message flow F is described as F= {P, C, T, D, J R } tuple. Each flow has priority (P), basic latency(C), flow period (T), deadline (D) and a release jitter (J R ). It is assumed that flow deadline is same as source task deadline which is same as task period.

For worst case schedulability analysis, end-to-end latencies are calculated considering maximum contention in the network. For this, worst case analysis proposed in [9] has been used, which predicts the worst case end-to-end latencies under a set of assumptions. The analysis proposed gives the maximum number of unschedulable tasks and traffic flows in the network, which is upper bound of unschedulability i.e., lower bound of schedulability. It assumes that, all the tasks of the application starts executing at the same time.

When multiple flows share the same physical link, lower priority flow gets contended by the higher priority flows. This interference can be of two types: Direct and Indirect. Direct interference defines interference by high-priority traffic flows when it shares the same path as the traffic flow under observation. The indirect interference is interference by a higher priority traffic flow that cause direct interference to the observed traffic flow and shares same path with the low-priority flows but not having direct interference with traffic flow under observation. div.head: IV. DEAMS ALGORITHM: AN OVERVIEW
div.p: Deadline and Energy Aware Task Mapping and Scheduling (DEAMS) algorithm guide mapping of an application on a NoC in a way to focus on minimization of energy and schedulability improvement. It uses heuristic which assures the confirmation of meeting task deadlines and minimization of communication energy consumption in dynamic applications. The accommodation of new application in dynamic scenario is proposed by considering the slack time of the tasks, so that system can respond to run-time situation in a better way. The algorithm decides a target Processor for ready task for execution depending on the spatial location and Earliest Available Time (EAT) of the running processing elements (PE). Categories of PE can be the either of the one on which execution of parent took place, or it's neighboring one. The task selection function (TSF) decides the sequence in which the ready tasks are allocated [6]. As DEAMS require run-time resource allocation, to minimize the execution time following simple heuristics has been used for task selection function TSF():Least Deadline First: TSF(t i ) = Min(dl i ) for all t i є Ready List

The DEAMS algorithm didn't consider the congestion in the network and priority of flows while mapping the incoming task. Schedulability obtained by considering flow priority, congestion in the network during mapping of an incoming task should be less than or equal to the schedulability obtained through DEAMS. Hence, in order to improve the accuracy of the results, modification has been done for the existing dynamic mapping algorithm DEAMS.As a part of the improvement, instead of slack time analysis, the worstcase analysis is used in DEAMS while mapping the incoming task to provide the lower bound of schedulability. The worst-case analysis considers the traffic conditions and flow priorities at a given instant. The modified algorithm chooses the processing element which gives the maximum schedulability considering the present traffic conditions. The desired schedulability results obtained through modified algorithm improves the accuracy of results while it remains less than the schedulability results obtained through DEAMS where congestion, flow priority assignment are not considered.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL WORK
div.p: The existing single processor based scheduling algorithms cannot find optimal flow priorities, in case of Network-on-Chip. The complexity of the flow priority assignment increases further in case of dynamic scenarios where the applications comes into the system or depart from the system at any time instant. In real-time NoC, some specific class of applications as illustrated in section-I, may have combination of both static and dynamic application. For static applications, flow priority assignment should be done at the first instance of application, which remains the same for other instances. Here, meta-heuristics like PSO, GA can be used for flow priority assignment. For dynamic applications, flow priorities are to be assigned considering the flows in existing application along with their dependencies applications and flows of incoming applications. In order to meet the above constraint, an existing static flow priority approach [18], GESA has been modified to work in dynamic scenarios.

div.head: A. Heuristics for Static Flow Priority Assignment:
div.p: Optimal flow priority assignment for the flows may improve schedulability. For static applications, resources allocated are fixed at design time, which cannot be changed in runtime. Here, we have applied two heuristics Earliest Deadline First, Shortest Job First and two meta-heuristics PSO, GA for flow priority assignments.

In meta-heuristics, the Goal is to explore the search space to find near-optimal solutions i.e., best flow priority assignment with maximum schedulability. Each particle in PSO and chromosome in GA is represented with an array of flow priorities, where the index of an array is the flow ID and value at corresponding index is the priority of the flow. Computationally meta-heuristics are expensive but performs significantly better compared to other heuristics, because meta-heuristics considers all the information at hand in fitness function (Worst case analysis). Also, among the meta-heuristics, PSO converges faster when compared to GA.

div.head: B. Applying GESA for priority assignment:
div.p: An existing static flow priority approach [18], GESA has been modified to work in dynamic scenarios. An undirectedgraph based exhaustive search algorithm is used to improve the efficiency of priority assignment process. For assessing degree of schedulability of the priority assignment using GESA, two functions are used to compute the lower and upper bounds of the worst-case response times. At each priority level of assignment, some flows are assigned with priorities and some are unassigned. With the unassigned flows, bounded analysis is performed using Direct and Indirect interference sets [17] to form candidate lists. The lower bound only considers the direct interfering flows, whereas the upper bound considers both direct and indirect interfering flows while computing the worst case traversal times for a given flow. The flows which are satisfying upper bound, said to be guaranteed schedulable, are made to form a list, while the flows satisfying the lower bound are said to be potentially schedulable, made to form a separate list. Using bounded analysis, GESA gives the relative priority ordering for the given subgraph. The first step to be done before applying the GESA is the construction of flow graph. The flow graph is an undirected dependency graph formed between the flows to show the flow dependencies or interferences. Whenever a flow is removed from the flow graph, multiple subgraphs are formed. According to Liu and Becker [18], if a node which is common with subgraphs is assigned a low priority of all nodes present in the subgraphs, flow priority assignment of one subgraph is independent from other subgraph. In order to check whether the current priority assignments are correct or not, a general schedulability test based on worst case analysis is applied after assigning priorities to all the flows. If the test fails, backtracking process is started by GESA. Backtracking process considers priority level which have multiple candidates i.e. there are more than one item in the list formed using bound analysis. When algorithms backtracks to a particular level P, all the flows with assigned priorities higher than or equal to P in that subgraph will be unassigned. Here, the subgraph refers to the subgraph present at the time of flow priority assignment of the flow assigned with P, which is failed in schedulability test. Then the algorithm assigns P to another candidate in the candidate list and continues to assign the remaining unassigned flows using the same procedure as before. If all the priority levels with multiple candidates are checked and the network still fails in the schedulability test, the GESA returns a result of unschedulability.

div.head: C. Working of proposed algorithm
div.p: Whenever flow priority assignment is to done for incoming applications, flow graph is constructed considering the existing applications. The flow priority assignment becomes more complex when incoming application overlaps i.e., tasks of incoming application shares the same cores with the tasks of existing applications. As a result, the flows in the incoming application will create additional interferences to the flows in the existing applications. In the proposed algorithm, GESA has been used to get the relative priority ordering between the unassigned flows. Some lower priority levels (buffer) are initially kept aside for partitioning the flow graph. At instance zero, relative priority of all the flows which are existing in the system is determined with GESA. Once the relative priorities are obtained, map the priority levels with an increment of buffer size i.e., priority level: 1 is mapped to priority level: (buffer+1). At any time instant, whenever the application is leaving the system, assigned priority levels will be freed up. In dynamic scenarios, whenever an application enters into the system, if any of the flows in incoming application do not share any links with the flows in existing applications, directly relative priorities of the flows in the existing application is determined and later mapped to the priority levels in a first-fit manner. Here, first-fit means all priorities are to be mapped on to the contiguous levels obtained, when searched from the priority level: (buffer+1). Also, if the flows in the incoming application shares links with the flows in the existing applications, the flows of incoming application which are sharing the links are assigned the lower priorities possible i.e., from buffer priority levels if available or, the lowest priority levels available outside the buffer priority levels.
The remaining flows are assigned the relative priorities using GESA and are mapped with first-fit manner.

div.head: D. Simulator Design and result validation:
div.p: In order to find out how tight the worst-case bound [20] is, a real time simulator was needed that could simulate a task graph, given its mapping and priority assignment. This simulator could give us the actual number of schedulable tasks and flows, which could be compared to that predicted by worst-case analysis. For a fixed set of parameters, the simulator was run for 50 milliseconds of execution of the application. The average schedulability in each 10 milliseconds was observed and plotted. This was seen to be well above the schedulability predicted by worst-case analysis. Therefore, the worst-case upper bound was validated by ensuring that the simulated real-time latencies are actually upper bounded by the worst case predictions.

div.head: VI. RESULTS AND COMPARISON
div.p: A. Dynamic Task Mapping Different task graphs has been generated considering hard or soft deadlines, and given as inputs to DEAMS algorithms. The results obtained from both approaches are compared with that of simulator. Worst-case analysis provides the lower bound of schedulability. Even though, the schedulability provided by DEAMS with worst-case gives lower values, but in real-time, these values can be higher than the obtained result and also this result is similar to result obtained from the simulator.

div.head: B. Dynamic Task Mapping and Flow Priority assignment
div.p: The proposed algorithm is invoked, whenever an application enters into the system. Here, task mapping is done by DEAMS algorithm, whereas flow priority assignment is done by modified GESA algorithm dynamically in run-time.

The following are the obtained average schedulability results tested on different task graphs, which are generated considering hard or soft deadlines. The proposed algorithm produces significantly better results compared to random mapping and GEAS or random priority assignment and DEAMS. Also, the obtained results from the proposed algorithm are compared with the average schedulability results obtained from simulator. The results produced from proposed algorithm are based on worst case analysis, simulator results are better compared to proposed algorithm because worst-case analysis gives lower bound of schedulability. Task mapping and Flow priority assignment is a complex problem as it affects the schedulability of the real-time systems. Generally, the resources are to be allocated in a separate manner for static and dynamic applications. In static scenarios, task mapping can be done by DEAMS while flow priority assignment with meta-heuristics like PSO, GA produces significantly better results compared to the heuristics like EDF, SJF. For better schedulability results in dynamic scenarios, an algorithm has been proposed using the existing algorithms GESA and DEAMS.

In the proposed algorithm, task mapping for the incoming applications will be done using DEAMS and the flows in the incoming applications are assigned the priorities using the modified GESA. The proposed algorithm is invoked, whenever an application enters into the system. A real-time simulator for dynamic scenarios is designed for comparing the schedulability results, which considers the dependencies between the flows unlike in worst case analysis. So far, optimization is done either considering flow priority assignment or mapping. Hence, this analysis can be extended to simultaneous optimization of both mapping and flow priorities. Also, instead of optimizing only mapping, flow priority assignment with a fixed routing algorithm for better schedulability, multiple routing algorithms can be used. In general, Most of the NoCs existing have limited number of virtual channels. Hence, in order to limit the number of virtual channels, all the work done can be implemented using priority sharing policies.
